title: The Most Expensive Word When You’re Chasing an Impossible Goal
author: Summer Mulder
summary: Mulder nominates 'yes' as the costliest word in business, more expensive than any failed campaign, bad hire or missed opportunity. She traces two episodes: early years in which saying yes to partnerships, projects and collaborations felt like momentum but was actually noise, and a later one in which a wobbling business with tight margins was pushed further under by a quick-fix 'opportunity' sold by an expert, which drained cash and added complexity while the root problem went unaddressed. Her analytical point is that the wrong yes never announces itself — it arrives feeling flattering, safe and opportune — so it cannot be caught by instinct and needs a rule instead. She explains why refusal gets harder as the goal gets bigger: the openness that helps at the start becomes a liability once every commitment competes with a single high-stakes objective. The tool she offers is a two-part filter tied to her own $100M target — does this move me toward the goal, and can only I do it — with delegate, delay or delete as the standing responses when either half fails. The closing accounting frame is the memorable part: every yes is a withdrawal from the resources the big goal needs, every no a deposit toward it.
points: The core distinction is between momentum and noise — accumulating commitments can feel like growth while actively fragmenting focus.
Mulder's warning that the wrong yes feels flattering and safe explains why founders cannot rely on gut feel and need an explicit filter.
The two-part test — does it move the goal, and can only I do it — is what turns the essay from a motivational riff into a usable decision rule.
Delegate, delay or delete is the standing answer for anything that fails the filter, which keeps the rule from collapsing into simple refusal.
Her second story is the sharper one: under financial pressure a yes can sabotage rather than merely delay, by consuming the reserves needed to fix the root cause.
quotes: I kept saying yes to partnerships, projects, and collaborations, thinking more was better. It felt like I was building momentum. In reality, I was just building noise.
It was that I needed to protect my focus from everything that wasn’t the big goal. When you’re chasing a big, unreasonable goal, the most dangerous thing you can do is say “yes” to the wrong thing.
It feels like opportunity. But a small yes to the wrong thing is a quiet agreement to delay the right thing.

Instead of ruthlessly protecting my resources for the moves that would fix the root problem, I said yes to an ‘opportunity’ that looked like a quick fix. I bought into the ‘expert’ telling me what I needed to do, and I agreed and tried to go as fast as possible.
We’re conditioned to believe that saying yes means we’re open, abundant, and ready for opportunity. And when you’re starting out, that mindset can help you grow.
When you have a big, audacious, impossible goal, every yes costs something. And that cost is almost always time you can’t get back.

Every yes is a withdrawal from the energy, focus, and resources you need for the big goal. Every no is a deposit toward it. When you’re chasing something that feels impossible, you don’t have the luxury of casual yeses.
